utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are continuing to sit today without Judge Williams, under the provisions of Rule 15 bis, subsection A. Good morning, witness. We are continuing with your examination-in-chief. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Simic. On Friday, we spoke about certain activities of the Crisis Staff that had to do with the organisation of farm production, assistance given to the local population, securing cattle feed, and so on. Please tell me this: During its existence, until the War Presidency was established, did the Crisis Staff also organise, together with relevant municipal organs, the sowing of plants and the harvesting? What do you know about these activities between April and July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war and nowadays as well, the municipal assembly would normally pass the plan of harvesting, and who was going to participate in those activities and so on. The operational activities that have to do with sowing of plants was done by the executive council of the municipality. In the times of war during 1992 and 1993, the Crisis Staff was aware of this, and I think that it even passed some decision that had to do with harvesting, but all of these matters were in the jurisdiction of the executive council and the executive council implemented this through commissioners and local communes. There were naturally many problems in that area because the machinery was damaged, there were no spare parts in sufficient quantities. They also lacked manpower. So this was faced with a lot of complications and problems, and very frequently the harvesting was disrupted by shelling and so on, so those people who were involved in harvesting were exposed to a significant risk, and all of this involved a lot of efforts. This -- however, despite of all that, this work was completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, do you know what obligations the municipality had with respect to the Ministry of Defence in terms of funds that had to be provided and personnel and so on? What do you know about this, about what is owed by the municipality in defence matters during wartime? Can you please explain to us what relationship exists between the municipality and other institutions during wartime.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since Posavina and Samac is a fertile wheat area and a lot of crops are grown there, crops that are used in order to feed the population and livestock, Samac municipality was actively involved in this, and they did discuss certain matters with the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you and ask you this -- can you tell me this: Does the municipality assist to the level that it is able to, or are there certain dues?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality assists to the level that it is able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But during wartime, there are certain requirements. There are certain plans that have to be met in terms of production and so on.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is how it is: The Ministry of Defence passed a decree regulating the war production matters, and every economic subject in particular had an obligation to draft a plan on wartime operation, which means that they had to list item by item all of the activities that had to be performed by the economic subject. At the same time, in addition to this production plan, the companies had to develop an organisational chart of employees to also specify what was the number of personnel that they required in order to meet their operational plan, and this was especially important in view of the work obligation that existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, please, another matter: In view of the obligations that existed with respect to the government, did the municipality implement certain measures in order to increase its budget? Did the municipality levy additional taxes during that period of time, 1992 and 1993? I'm now interested only in the matters that fall under the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since there were insufficient funds throughout that time and since additional funds had to be secured, the municipality did take certain measures in that respect. There was a regulation on municipal taxes that was passed. I've already told you that the executive council was in charge of these regulations and their enforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, please, in the month of May 1992, what was the main topic, what was the main problem facing the Crisis Staff in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May of 1992, the times were very hard, if one can say so. Perhaps April was harder, but May was just as hard because a number of terrible problems had accumulated by then. Throughout the entire month of May, there was a very intense shelling of that area. There was a terrible situation internally, terrible pressure that was caused by shelling, and as a result of that a large number of Serb residents, especially women, children, the elderly, and the sick, had left the area. I think that even after one shelling, in mid-May, a large number of buses carrying Serb residents, mostly women and children, left the area and sought shelter in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am sorry to interrupt you. During that period of time, was the region of Samac municipality left by other residents, not just Serb residents?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. It probably was, because the situation at that time was unbearable. One could see that with respect to ordinary people, with respect to all people who lived in the area. One could see how people were under tremendous psychological pressure. At the time there were no agencies or services that dealt with that problem, but I know that a term was widely used and at the time entered our language. And I've never used that -- I've never heard that term before, but the term was that the person went nuts, which meant that somebody was unable to maintain rational composure and we had a lot of problems with psychological -- a lot of people with psychological problems. Therefore, the Crisis Staff was faced with a variety of problems. I remember that on one occasion a man came and said that he had three or four children whom he didn't know -- for whom he didn't know who they belonged to. They stayed with relatives in Samac. The parents of these children who were refugees were in Odzak municipality, and the children had to take care of themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you notice in March and April of 1992, in view of increased tensions, did you observe whether during that period of time the population of Samac also left the area?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population of Samac from all three ethnic groups, meaning Serbs, Croats, and Muslims, started leaving Samac municipality perhaps as early as one year prior to the conflict, and this culminated in the time immediately before the breakout of war. It seems to me that there was a trend --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you give us some numbers? I know it's hard to give assessments, but give us an approximate idea.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there were several thousands of people that left the area, from all three ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In May of 1992, what was the number of Serb refugees in Samac, if you know, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May I would say there was several thousand of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Refugees from where?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from all areas, that is, from the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. A large number of them was from Gradacac. There were many of them from Odzak as well, and many other places in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also the neighbouring municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what did municipal organs such as the Crisis Staff and executive council do regarding this problem? How did they solve the problems that stemmed from the influx of large number of refugees into the municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The refugees were housed in those facilities that could be obtained at the time. That means that they were housed in Serb houses but also in housing facilities that became vacant after their previous tenants had left. Certain apartments became vacant, and refugees were settled in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did the Crisis Staff do regarding that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did not do anything regarding that. It was not active in that area. I will repeat: The Crisis Staff did not have its professional staff. It did not have its apparatus. This was handled by services that were in charge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the activity of the Crisis Staff in May of 1992 regarding the problems faced by Serbs in Odzak? You spoke at length about this, but could you please summarise it for us. What were the activities taken by the Crisis Staff and how was this matter resolved, this matter with Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that the International Red Cross facilitated, or rather, participated in the first exchange of residents from that area. I think that there were a number of these exchanges, as a result of which a large number of residents from Odzak municipality came to the other side. I assume that there were some other mechanisms. Some people managed to flee from imprisonment and from that area. Of course, there were not many such cases. Also, a large number of residents went into other areas where the Croatian side held power. Some of them even went into Croatia. Some people went to Slavonski Brod.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What people do you have in mind now?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean residents of Serb ethnicity who were originally from Odzak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where were their relatives?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their relatives were in Samac municipality. This uniting of families occasionally was quite a long-lasting process. Some families were separated for quite a long time, sometimes during the entire period of war. I think that there were exchanges that took place as late as 1994 and 1995. For example, if one member of the family was imprisoned in April or May of 1992 and then exchanged in 1995, that means that the family was separated for three entire years. And there were many cases like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was a decision passed in May to isolate Croats? Was such a decision passed by the Crisis Staff? Also, a decision to place Croats in vital facilities in town; do you know anything about this decision?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, such decision was never passed. It borders on --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You don't have to comment on this. Were Croats placed in vital facilities in the town of Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's not letting the witness finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because my intention was to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I think the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- speed up things as much as possible. He can clarify that in cross-examination. I mean, Your Honour, I don't know what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I thought that counsel was right to tell the witness not to comment but just to give evidence in terms of facts, what he knows and what he knew. Yes, please, Mr. Pantelic proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So I'm asking you the following: Were citizens of Samac who were of Croat ethnicity placed in vital facilities in town in May 1992 or in any other period in 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such horrible things never happened in the territory of the municipality of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Tell me, did some other horrible things happen? Do you know anything about killing non-Serbs in Crkvina, which was committed by some volunteers? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any official information on this, which means that I never found out anything about this either orally or in writing through any official channels. However, I did hear about this. After the already-mentioned volunteer Lugar -- well, this was, say, a month and a half or two after that event, after he was in the investigating prison in Banja Luka -- rather, the military investigative prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to May 1992. You were involved in information. You were a member of the Crisis Staff, et cetera. What do you personally know about this event which I just referred to; that is to say, the killing of non-Serb civilians in Crkvina? We are talking about May 1992. What do you know about that? And if you found out, when did you find out?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May, I didn't know anything. I didn't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. At the Crisis Staff, was this discussed? Was it discussed among the people in town? This is not a small, minor matter, after all. Do try to remember.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not a minor matter, but it was not discussed in town. I assume that whoever committed such a horrible crime, that is to say, the killing of civilians of non-Serb ethnicity, would also be capable of shutting the mouths of those who would spread such news.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So really --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that. That's nothing more than speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Simic, please focus on what you saw. Do not assume anything. So we are discussing facts.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Look, if you didn't understand -- you said that some -- that you assumed that somebody would shut the mouths of those, et cetera, et cetera, but stay away from such assumptions. Please focus. Tell me, what was the relationship between the municipal authorities and the volunteers in the period between April and June 1992? Can you give us some of your assessments of the situation and so on. Was it friendly? Was it this? Was it that? How could you classify it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot testify to anything in this regard because volunteers were within the structure of the armed forces. So the Crisis Staff from that point of view, with regard to this matter, never looked into anything, never discussed anything, so I cannot define this relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did Stevan Todorovic report to the Crisis Staff on the measures taken, if any, by the police regarding what happened in Crkvina? I'm referring to the killing of a number of non-Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Stevan Todorovic never reported to the Crisis Staff about this crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Another thing I'm interested in -- well, first of all, actually, tell me, when did you first find out about this, about what crimes were allegedly committed by Stevan Todorovic? I'm asking you personally as an individual.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out about that only from Dragan Lukac's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you read the book?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now exactly, but it was after the war was over. Now, was it 1996 or 1997? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you in contact with Stevan Todorovic? Did you talk to him after you read Dragan Lukac's book? I mean, after all, you came from the same town. Did you ask him whether what Lukac wrote was true? Could you explain this to us.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was no longer in Samac by then.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know when charges were brought against Stevan Todorovic, when he was indicted by this Tribunal -- or rather, the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you know about this in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say anything with certainty, but after a few months --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1995, was there a state of war there?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Until when?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until the war was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In November 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, are you personally aware of the confession made by Stevan Todorovic in these proceedings before this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I know that the media carried some information to the effect that he did admit certain things. But what it was exactly, I don't know. I'm not aware of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. If I tell you that Stevan Todorovic confessed that he committed a certain number of crimes, that is to say, beatings, sexual harassment, and let's say killings too. With regard to these confessions made before this Tribunal, did he inform the Crisis Staff about what he was doing in 1992 and 1993? Throughout those two year, did he inform the Crisis Staff of these things that he later admitted to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stevan Todorovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a little bit confusing because he's saying he doesn't know exactly what he admitted. If he -- if you tell him "assume the following," he admitted the following, then I think you could say that -- ask that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What do you mean? Because counsel has said "beatings, sexual harassment, and let's say killings too." If you look at the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'm sorry. I'll withdraw the objection. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic did not tell the Crisis Staff of any such thing when he was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After the end of 1993, in the period after that, did he ever report to the municipal government authorities about the crimes he had committed?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. This sounds nonsensical to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would somebody who had committed such a thing inform somebody about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object once again to speculation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's either he did or he never did, and I think the witness has answered. Can we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, do you know something about the work of the commission of the Ministry of the Interior in relation to certain activities, certain official activities of Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the commission's name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the commission of the MUP of Republika Srpska that investigated the work or the activities of Stevan Todorovic in Samac? I mean, if you know, you know. If you don't --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't even know of the existence of such a commission, let alone these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. What do you personally know about the event that took place in May 1992 concerning the temporary detention of a number of non-Serb inhabitants at the stadium in Crkvina? Do you know of this incident?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. I only know that the Crisis Staff always made a distinction between military and police activities on the one hand and the civilian activities that the Crisis Staff was involved in on the other hand. At sessions of the Crisis Staff though, the only thing that was done -- or rather, the only thing that was discussed was the following: To try, after Serb civilians were taken prisoner in Odzak, to prevent the possible outbreak of Serb extremism. As for military and police affairs, the Crisis Staff did not involve itself in that at all. I note that the president of the Crisis Staff, Blagoje Simic, always said, "Let everyone do his own work. Let the police do their own work, the military have their own province of work, and the civilian government authorities have their own line of work." So with regard to these particular matters, I know very little, barely a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what you personally know about the following: The Crisis Staff and some members of the Crisis Staff in the period from the end of May until the beginning of June 1992, did it take part in any way in the appointment of certain military commanders in the territory of the municipality of Samac? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff never had the authority or the powers or was it stipulated in any piece of legislation that the Crisis Staff could do such a thing, namely, appoint military people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, that is the official relationship, which is obvious. However, were there any unofficial attempts to try to impose upon the Crisis -- to have the Crisis Staff impose certain personnel changes within the military units in the municipality? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything about that. I have no information about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what military formation was active in the territory of the municipality of Samac in the period from the end of May, beginning of June, and further on? What was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, which had within it lower-level units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: From a military point of view, who comprised the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade? Where did these soldiers come from?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The soldiers were the local Serb population and citizens of other ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within the 2nd Posavina Brigade, were there any active commanding officers of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When was this? When was this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the 19th of May, there were no more JNA officers, except for those who originally came from that area. And then they joined the ranks of the Army of Republika Srpska, which was established later. But I cannot give a complete answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. But can you say whether you know when the Army of Republika Srpska was established?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, you personally as an individual and as a member of the Crisis Staff, what do you know about the existence of a camp for non-Serb inhabitants in the village of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any camp in the village of Zasavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You read the book of Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You also read newspaper articles, et cetera. Could you describe Zasavica for me. What did this look like? Was Zasavica an area that had barbed wire around it? Were there any watchtowers? Tell me everything you know about Zasavica. Who was in Zasavica, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zasavica is a village on the outskirts of Samac, 4 or 5 kilometres away from Samac itself, on the banks of the Bosna River. When you drive along the road from Samac to Modrica, then you will pass by that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's fine. We know that. Could you just describe for us what I asked you.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go in there, so what I saw from this road -- I mean, the Samac-Modrica road was not unusual in any way. I didn't see anything unusual, and I'm not aware of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. What were the activities of the Crisis Staff in relation to Odzak? What do you know about Odzak? We are talking about 1992 onwards. Let me ask you another thing, actually: In the period from April 1992 onwards, under whose control was Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Odzak was under the control of the Croat side -- or rather, it was the HVO that was in control there from a military point of view, and that is when --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's what you heard. So until when?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the month of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the Army of Republika Srpska liberated the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Which unit?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was the role of the Samac Municipal Crisis Staff relating to Odzak at that time?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role was as much as possible to help those imprisoned people there who were exposed to terrible torture.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When we're talking about the break-through of the corridor -- and now we're talking about the 1st Krajina Corps, which controlled that area -- could you please tell me what happened in the period of July and onwards. What was the role of the Samac Municipal Crisis Staff regarding Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military administration was introduced in Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when did you find that out?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the date, but at that time I found out that military administration was introduced there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: -- To rearrange my exhibits there. So if you allow me -- I do apologise personally, because I -- I didn't find enough -- I am going to explore some issue now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have a break of 10 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll break for 10 minutes. --- Break taken at 10.21 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, you said that the military administration was introduced in Odzak in July 1992 by the 1st Krajina Corps. Could you please tell me what the role of the Samac Crisis Staff was in relation to this military administration specifically. Did this military administration have any requests or demands? How did this function? How did the Municipal Crisis Staff of Samac direct its activities? What happened? Were these partner relations? How did this function? Could you please tell us what you know about this period.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area on the territory of the Odzak municipality, production was to have started up and all the economic facilities were supposed to begin to function. So in this operative sense, it was more a job for the executive authorities rather than the Crisis Staff. So I wouldn't really be able to tell you anything more on that topic. I really don't have any information about that. I don't know what was happening. I think -- no, I know for certain that I went to the territory of the Odzak municipality only once in that period, and that was with journalists from an English TV station which was making a report about the rapes of Serb women during the HVO administration in the territory of the Odzak municipality. I know the name of one woman who was featured in that report, but I wouldn't like to say it publicly, but I could provide that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll go back to the issues we are concerned with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, could you please tell me, if you have any information about that, who was heading the military administration in Odzak? Do you know the name of the person, the rank, the institution? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an officer, but I can't remember his first and last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did anyone from the Crisis Staff in Samac participate in this military administration in Odzak? Was anyone from Samac a part of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A body, which I think was called the council, the council of the military administration, had as its member a person called Savo Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Savo Popovic, in view of the fact that he was a member of the Crisis Staff, and then as of July 1992 was a member of the War Presidency. Did he take part in the work of the municipal bodies in Samac in the activities of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Savo Popovic, when he moved to this duty no longer appeared at meetings of the Crisis Staff -- at least, I don't remember seeing him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. That was until mid-July that the Crisis Staff functioned. After that it was the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me if he sent any reports. Was he in the capacity of an officer of the municipal administration of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information of him sending any reports to the civilian authorities or --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When I say "the civilian authorities of Samac," I mean by that the certain bodies, the executive board and the War Presidency. Did they have any effect on the military authorities who were heading the military administration in Odzak in 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities in Samac did not have any influence, even over the lower levels of the military structure, and particularly not over this one, nor could it in that sense --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could the Samac civilian authorities issue orders to the military administration in Odzak about what should be done, how things should be organised, and so on?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities could not issue any orders. Although, I think that there was some kind of decree at the ministry level about some duties which could be carried out in those circumstances. But I don't have any information or knowledge about that, about how this functioned in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And could you please explain this concept of military administration. Based on the example in Odzak, what does this -- what did this mean? If you know.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question that I would not really like to go into and this term "military administration," I couldn't really define it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did this Crisis Staff and later the War Presidency of the Municipality of Samac in any way participate in the organising of the work duty in Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that it did, but I don't have any information on that. There were many destroyed houses there, factories also, and other facilities, and I assume that work was being done in that regard, but I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Serb refugees from the municipality of Odzak in the course of 1992 and 1993, if you know anything about that, did they come back to their homes?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serb refugees who fled in the first half of 1992, at the time when that area was controlled by the Croatian side, in late 1992 and early 1993 and in the course of 1993 returned to their homes, to their houses in Serb villages in the territory of the municipality of Odzak, and they did this in large numbers. They repaired their houses there and were creating conditions to resume living there, and they stayed there until 1995, when --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What happened in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1995 there was again a mass exodus because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Of whom?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the Serb population because, according the Dayton Peace Accords, the Odzak municipality was to go to the Federation, to become a part of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Serb population, afraid that they will not again be exposed to the same things that they were exposed to in 1992 -- so again in a terrible mass exodus moved out to the territory of the municipality of Samac, Modrica, and other municipalities within Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the course of July 1992 and onwards, was there any Croat or Muslim population in the territory of the Odzak municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During July. I'm talking about the period where the corridor was broken through. Do you have any information about the Croat population and the Muslim population in the municipality of Odzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that there were any, due to the offensive -- the citizens also were in exodus from that area, and they were fleeing before the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the municipal authorities in Samac have any influence over the movement of Muslims and Croats from the municipality of Odzak in July 1992 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipality of Samac did not and could not have anything to do with the movement of the Croat and Muslim population from the municipality of Odzak.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more specific. You said "municipality." That's a pretty wide term. I was talking about the municipal civil authority. So could you be more specific because of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian authorities of the municipality of Samac did not in any way influence nor could they influence the exodus of the Croat and Muslim population during combat operations in mid-1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of Samac municipality and later on the War Presidency -- so in order not to keep repeating, I'm now referring to the officials that were members of the Crisis Staff and later on the War Presidency. So did they ever in their sessions and meetings, ever pass any decisions on forcible removal of the non-Serb residents from their apartments and houses in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Crisis Staff sessions, such discriminatory matters were never discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Blagoje Simic advocated such ideas outside of the sessions?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blagoje Simic never advocated such ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the Crisis Staff and later on the War Presidency regarding the arrests of some non-Serb residents in Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian organs of Samac municipality never got involved in the affairs of the military, police, and other services if they did not have any competencies in these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic, as chief of police, was he an ex officio member of the Crisis Staff up until mid-July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic was chief of police, and he was never a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did he ever attend sessions of the Crisis Staff? And if so, what was his role there?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. Stevan Todorovic attended sessions of the Crisis Staff, just as he attended all sessions that he was allowed to attend. Stevan Todorovic is a kind of a man who liked to impose himself and to go to places where he was not desired, where he was not a member of a certain group. But that's the kind of man he was. He wanted to appear in all places and among other things, he would also attend sessions of the Crisis Staff. Sometimes he also submitted reports that had to do with the competencies of the Crisis Staff, meaning what was outside of the investigative actions of police.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was Stevan Todorovic a member of the War Presidency of Samac Municipality?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Stevan Todorovic was not a member of the War Presidency, and he couldn't have been one because that would then create a confusion between the legislative and executive branch of government. He reported directly to the minister for his actions, and the War Presidency was a civilian organ that existed in lieu of the municipal assembly in wartime.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Stevan Todorovic demand from the Crisis Staff of Samac municipality during its existence to provide additional facilities for prisoners who were under his jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of him putting such demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was the problem of proceedings that were launched against some non-Serb residents -- and by this, I mean criminal proceedings -- ever discussed at the Crisis Staff? Specifically, did Stevan Todorovic ever report to the Crisis Staff on these matters?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I repeat, the Crisis Staff never got involved in police matters, including these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did he then on his own initiative report to the municipal organs because he as chief of police had a duty to report on the matters within his jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic always used to say that civilians shouldn't meddle into things that do not concern them, meaning the police matters, and that was accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know when was it that some detained non-Serbs were transferred to the jurisdiction of the military prosecutor's office -- or military judiciary in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when this took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what do you know about the proceedings that were launched in the military court in Banja Luka? Was the War Presidency in any way involved in this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency only received a brief piece of information saying that a group of volunteers had committed certain deeds which were investigated by the military organs and that these individuals were in the investigative prison in Banja Luka. I didn't know specifically what this was all about. At that time, I had thoughts that this was in some way connected to the crime in Crkvina. However, I didn't have any specific information about what it was all about except for what I could read in the papers. I think that at the time the paper from Belgrade, "Vecernje Novosti" reported on this. These articles were authored by Banja Luka reporter Boro Maric [phoen]. However, these article were not sufficient to provide in-depth information about what that involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What were -- what was the information circulated in Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were all kinds of rumours circulating in Samac. It was said that those volunteers, due to crimes committed in Crkvina, due to harassment that the population was exposed to, due to looting, were as a result of that imprisonment. And that's what the rumours said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the civilian organs in Samac organise looting and plundering of property in broad terms, the property belonging to the non-Serb population? I'm now referring to 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did civilian organs of government in Samac, according to your knowledge, organise plundering in the territory of Samac municipality and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection again. It's the same question. It's still --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It's the same question, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: It's still leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What do you know about cases of plundering in the territory of Samac and Odzak in the course of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian authorities did not naturally organise, nor did they participate --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe it's time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Let him finish the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilian authorities did not participate in any actions that had to do with plundering and crime, on the contrary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1992 and 1993, were there any incidents of plundering and any other crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plundering and crime is in my mind something that goes with war, and there were cases of that naturally; however, there were no cases of organised plundering, especially not plundering organised by civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was it organised by some other authorities, some other kinds of authorities?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm convinced that it was, because there is a lot of organised crime in Bosnia and Herzegovina even nowadays; therefore, I think that just like nowadays, in the times of war it was organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Move to strike, Your Honour, on speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It has no value, of course. Could we have a break, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And we'll continue our proceedings at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, before the break, you spoke about the cases of plundering and that that was a result of the hostilities and the war. Now, tell me, please, did the municipal authorities in any way organise the removal of private property from the private homes of non-Serb residents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, once again, this isn't cross-examination. He can ask what role did the municipality or the executive take. But this is just -- he's giving statements and he's really asking for a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic, please reorganise your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the municipal organs, municipal authorities point out to certain negative actions of military authorities? And if so, when and on what occasion?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, were there any cases of unlawful actions?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have occasion to see a single document, nor did I ever -- was officially informed of this, nor did I hear what the soldiers of the 1st Krajina Corps did. Therefore, I was not aware of any such actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, in the period up until July of 1992, were there any cases where other organs used the name of the Crisis Staff in view of the scope of tasks that had to be completed and in view of the special circumstances during that time? Do you have any information regarding that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On what occasions did that take place? What were the circumstances surrounding it and what was the reason behind this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period when the president of the Crisis Staff, Blagoje Simic, was wounded and while he was recovering, there was a possibility for some other organs to use the name and seal of the Crisis Staff and perhaps pass a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. It doesn't help us at all. The witness doesn't know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour. I will go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, please, was there a stamp of the Crisis Staff with the name of the Crisis Staff on it, or was a different kind of stamp used with some other text?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The stamp had the following text on it -- the stamp did not have a text indicating "Crisis Staff" on it. Rather, the text was "The Serb Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation." And later on, it simply said, "The Municipal Assembly of Samac," once the Pelagicevo municipality became a separate entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, how many stamps were there of the Serb Municipality of Samac and Pelagicevo under formation? Can you tell us which organs used that stamp?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that I saw reflected that that stamp was used by the Crisis Staff, occasionally by the executive council, and I also saw one document which indicated that the police had used that stamp as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Regarding the schools and their operation, you told us that due to war breaking out, the schools were closed in springtime and then resumed their work in the fall. Can you tell us, please, when did that happen? When did the schools resume their work? In which facilities?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1991/1992 school year was brought to an end in April of 1992. Despite the fact that the students did not attend classes until the official end of the school year, the classes were brought to an end in April of 1992, and then in the 1992/1993 school year, the classes started at the end of 1992. The existing facilities could not be used for classes because the building of the elementary school was destroyed, completely ruined, and it could not be used to hold classes, whereas the building of the secondary school was of a provisional nature, and therefore it wasn't safe to hold classes there due to constant shelling. Therefore, classes, both in elementary and in secondary school, were held in other facilities which were safer. The teachers in the secondary school during that school year travelled to various sites and held classes there because that was safer, both for students and for teachers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what sites those were. Can you tell us where classes were held.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Classes were held in following sites: In Samac, there were two or three such sites that were considered safe locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what were these.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two or three facilities that had been used before as catering facilities and then were made into classrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And outside of Samac territory?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sites outside of Samac were Crkvina, Zasavica, Slatina, and Obudovac Dva.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In relation to information, you spoke about the bulletin. The bulletin was -- how should I put this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: May I ask for correction of the transcript. It is on page 30, line 12. Here it says Obudovac Dva. This would imply probably that it is the name of town. But actually he said that there were two premises in Obudovac, in the village of Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In terms of the transcript, when you mentioned Obudovac, what did you say exactly?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obudovac Dva is a local commune. There was Obudovac I, Obudovac Jedan, and Obudovac Dva, Obudovac II. This is a settlement that is divided into two local communes along administrative lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell me, this bulletin was a printed matter that was distributed in town. Tell me, how often was this bulletin published and what was it printed on?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bulletin was an information leaflet. Its dimensions were A4. It was printed in a rather obsolete technology on a so-called copier. Let me explain this a bit. A typewriter would be used to type out the text on the master copy, and then this master copy would be put into this copier machine and then that way it would be printed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was the printing done?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information service had its two rooms at the heating plant, that is to say, where the Crisis Staff had its premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What were the contents of this bulletin? Like, what did it report about?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This bulletin published news about the front line, what was going on at the front line, then also information concerning what the civilian authorities did. Also, it carried some texts from other newspapers. From time to time, it also carried information about what the media of the other side were reporting on. So it was pretty short, and for the most part it was like an information leaflet on a single A4 page, and it was copied in, say, 30 to 50 copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How frequently was it published?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, that is to say, during the first 20 or so days, it was published every day. Perhaps two or three times, a day or two would be skipped. And then, say, once or twice a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Is the "Koridor" a sequel to this bulletin or is it something quite different? I'm referring to the "Koridor" newspaper.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the "Koridor" is not a sequel to this leaflet. The "Koridor" had been conceived as a more serious newspaper -- magazine, rather, with many more pages. It was printed in a better way, and also its editorial concept was more sophisticated. So it was a real newspaper in the real sense of the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You personally, as you moved about town, did you hear the screams and the beatings of people in the TO? I'm talking about 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, at that time I never strolled in the streets of town because quite simply that was not a safe thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You mean the whole of 1992 and the whole of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992 was that way throughout, but 1993 was already safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about 1992? You started explaining this. You said that you didn't stroll about the streets.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Only when I went to work. But that was very fast walking, a very dynamic thing, because sometimes I would experience shelling on my way to work or from work and it would not be easy to find shelter at the same moment. So I didn't hear any screams or anything unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you hear any loud singing from the TO premises?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear any singing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: At sessions of the Crisis Staff and later at sessions of the War Presidency, was there any mention regarding the passing of certain decisions that jeopardised the basic human rights of the non-Serb population in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'd object to that again, Your Honour. Very leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How would you describe the decisions of the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency during 1992? What was the objective of these decisions? How would you characterise them?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have understood your question. What happened at Crisis Staff meetings was discussed in terms of the subject matter involved in the following way: In every decision the highest civilisational standards were observed. They incorporated the democratic rights of citizens, not only of Serb ethnicity, of course, but all others as well. And at sessions of the Crisis Staff in this way the discussions were held. This was truly taken into account. However, on the other hand, when I looked at some decisions, I saw that they were drafted pretty clumsily, in terms of style. Some of the wording was even ambiguous. So this is something that I ascribed to a lack of concentration on the part of the staff members, especially when there were shellings and different situations. Probably under this kind of pressure, a word or two would be included in terms of something that had not been discussed at the sessions. So I did notice such things in documents, but I know for sure that even if it did happen, that some bad formulation would be included. It never carried any weight in practice really. Very often, actually -- let me try to be brief. There were things that testified to a popular belief, and that is that paper will suffer anything. Sometimes there were poor definitions, but this did not really have any practical effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Finally, let me ask you about this period when you cooperated with Dr. Blagoje Simic. How would you describe his work and generally speaking him as a personality during that period?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've known Blagoje Simic since my early childhood, so I think I do know his personality. During this period, during the functioning of the Crisis Staff, that is, he tried investing maximum efforts to get things moving in the best possible way. He always insisted on everyone doing his own job; that is to say, that he insisted on that very often. For instance, if somebody would go into an area that he thought was not his, he would always repeat the following: "No, let him do his job and we're going to do our job." So he did not like any kind of interference in the affairs of others. At the same time, I think that he got into politics very young and that sometimes, since the situation was difficult, he could not always find an adequate answer to some problems. But he made a maximum effort, and in terms of everything he did, I think he was guided by these principles: That it should be fair, that it should not be to anyone's detriment, that there should be no discrimination involved, that no one should be hurt and nobody's human rights should be infringed upon, any kind of human right, material, economic, social, et cetera. And very often people from his party, the SDS, accused him of keeping a lot of people from the opposition in the structures of government. He would then answer that everything that was decided had to be an expression of the will expressed in the previous selections and that there is a place for everyone there and the more people are involved, the more wisdom is involved. He tried to engage this wisdom in the best possible way in order to contribute to the highest principles that everybody was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I don't know if I asked you this already, but in 1992 and 1993 you were a member of which party?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Liberal Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have finished my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any questions by any other counsel from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Defence of Miroslav Tadic, I state that we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: On behalf of Mr. Zaric's Defence, we do not wish to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well. Cross-examination by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Phil Weiner. I work for the Office of the Prosecutor. I'm going to ask you some questions. Sir, your position on the Crisis Staff involved information, did it not?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And your job was to obtain information, disseminate information to the press and public; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you were the person who dealt with the press, whether it was the television, the radio, the newspaper press, giving them information, assisting them when they came to visit?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I and other members of the information staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, today you testified on page 9 of today's transcript about the Crkvina massacre. You stated, "In May, I didn't know anything about it" -- I'm sorry. "In May I didn't know anything. I didn't know anything about it." Was that your testimony today?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the month of May, I did not know anything about that massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And then you indicated that "It was not discussed in the town." That was your testimony today, correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I didn't hear anything about it in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you also said, "It was not discussed in town." I'm quoting you. When you were asked how could you not know about it, it was -- "this was not a small, minor matter after all. Do you remember?" Your answer, "It was not a minor answer, but it was not discussed in town." Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I had not heard anything about this matter in town. I didn't hear it being discussed by people. And at the same time, I did not have any official information about this. I didn't hear that any such thing had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that everyone in Bosanski Samac was aware of this massacre of the non-Serb population and were discussing it in the town? Isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Why your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, he already said that he was not aware about the issues. And how he could speculate what was the -- in the topics of the other circle of people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. No. This is cross-examination, and the Prosecution can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yeah. But he can be more specific, I mean, in questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. There is a difference between examination-in-chief and cross-examination, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I am aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it a fact that everyone in Bosanski Samac was aware of this massacre of non-Serb civilians and were discussing it in the town?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that I didn't know. As for some circles or some group, I mean, whether somebody knew about that, I cannot really confirm any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Miroslav Tadic gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 27th of March, 1998, which is Exhibit 139. At page 7 of that statement, he's asked, "Maybe the --"

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not object when the statements of other persons were quoted, when Blagoje Simic was concerned because he's an accused person who heard what the witnesses said. However, I do object because during the Prosecution case, witnesses were not being in a position to have other people's statements shown to them. So why would this be the case now? Would the same rule please be applied?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, it can't be applied because the material which the Prosecution is referring to was the interview of an accused in this case. So the Prosecution can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He is questioned at page 7: "Maybe the most notorious incident he was involved in was the killing of 16 or 17 men at the warehouse in Crkvina on the 7th of May, 1992. I know that this killing was widely known by people in the area, and I assume that that was brought to your attention." Answer by Mr. Tadic: "Yes. It could not have been avoided, not to hear about it. Even housewives who had spent the war in cellars heard about it. That was something unimaginable at the time, that someone would commit such a crime for no apparent reason, and that obviously placed a terrible shadow over all the relationships in Samac." Sir, do you know any reason why Miroslav Tadic would say that everyone knew about that if it wasn't true? Do you know of any reason, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot know what Mr. Tadic was guided by when he gave such a statement, but I know for a fact that housewives and so on, a broad circle of people in Samac, knew this. And if this were so, I would also probably know about it. I don't believe that story about the housewives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's move on. Are you aware that the defendant Simo Zaric provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on April 2nd, 1998, which is Exhibit 141? Are you aware that he stated - and he's referring to a meeting he had just had on that morning with Dr. Blagoje Simic, also a defendant, and he, it says, referring to Blagoje Simic, said that "He would call a meeting of the Crisis Staff and do what his job was." Do you recall a meeting of the Crisis Staff in relation to the Crkvina massacre?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember because a meeting was never convened at that time, when the Crisis Staff operated, in order to discuss this topic. So I am absolutely unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that last week Dr. Blagoje Simic testified when asked on direct examination, at page 12.289, "Please tell me, was something officially done after the incident?"

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We asked all competent authorities, especially the judiciary to process that, to bring them to trial, to try them and to punish them. Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, I would like to object. The witness is now being told about a statement by the witness from examination-in-chief, which was never allowed to the Defence to tell a witness something that another witness stated during trial. If we want to have equality of sides, then this kind of -- this way of asking the question should not be permitted. Perhaps this question could be asked in another way. Several times the Prosecution -- Your Honour, I cannot tell you any more, but we tried on several occasions to ask during cross-examination a witness about things that other witnesses said and the Prosecution objected to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But it did happen several times. I cannot give you examples now. This was during the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you asked us to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- rephrase such questions, if you remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I recall that. What I'm asking you is the materials the Prosecution is referring to, they refer to which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now the Prosecution has changed the statement of Blagoje Simic. It is presenting what the accused said as a witness during the examination-in-chief. At that moment he was a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he's being presented -- what he said is being presented as he said it when he was a witness. I understand that in this way they would like to undermine the witness by telling him about what another witness said during the actual proceedings, not a written statement but something that a witness said during the actual proceedings in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: When an accused person decides to give evidence, he still remains an accused person. And for all intents and purposes, he is treated as an accused person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the Prosecution will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Dr. Blagoje Simic later testified that when he referred to "we," he's referring to the Crisis Staff. Now, sir, he indicated that the Crisis Staff took actions. Do you know any reason why he would say it if it wasn't true? You were a member of that Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This can be explained in the following way: It is quite possible that Dr. Blagoje Simic knew about this event and that he informed some members of the Crisis Staff about it and that they took some steps regarding this matter. But I know for a fact that the Crisis Staff as a body, as a forum, did not have any information about this nor did it discuss this. And as far as I know, there is no document that would indicate anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, but you can only speculate as to why Dr. Blagoje Simic would have said that, indicated that the Crisis Staff acted. You cannot give a positive answer.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But when he uses the term "we," that does not mean the Crisis Staff as a forum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, that was his testimony.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Let's move on to another issue and let's see how your memory is with this. Sir, could you look at Exhibit 71, please -- P71. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you have a chance to look at that document?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you please look at it.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it now. Now I know it. But I haven't seen it before, nor was it ever presented at any meeting of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any order by the Crisis Staff -- or any similar order issued by the Crisis Staff? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any order by the Crisis Staff or issued by the Crisis Staff to isolate non-Serb civilians in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not familiar with any decision, order, or any other document which would talk about any discriminatory acts. This was simply something that was not there and it was not part of any decision-making at the sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, are you aware of any large-scale arrest and detention of Croat citizens in May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any mass arrests in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you indicated this morning that a decision of this type - and you used the word "horrible," would be horrible - and you just used the word "discriminatory." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What should it be exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you just indicated that this type of act, isolating or arresting large numbers of non-Serb civilians, would be discriminatory. And earlier today on direct examination you indicated that it would be a horrible act. Are those your characterisations of such an act, horrible, discriminatory?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If people are arrested individually or en masse, and there is no underlying intention to protect these people, then of course that is horrible, and I stand by that term.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, you indicated that you were involved with the radio station -- you were involved with the radio station in Bosanski Samac, correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bosanski Samac radio station had its editor-in-chief, and I did cooperate with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How often in the month of April -- in the months of April, May, and June did you visit the radio station in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the information service of the Crisis Staff issued a bulletin, it did very rarely anything in that domain. I can't remember. Perhaps it was once or twice that I was there at the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's just intervention to the transcript. 44, page and line 3/4. Maybe I didn't hear, but is that 1992 or 1993? In order to clarify the period, maybe for the transcript, for the purposes of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I can clear that up, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the year of 1992, how often did you visit the radio station in May? Let's take the month of May.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely. I didn't have any need to go there, to the radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And you know the radio station is right near the schools, the primary school and the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
