utterances.text: And were you aware in May and June and July -- let's say from May through the summer -- how the primary and secondary schools were being used?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know why the elementary and the secondary schools were being used. The elementary school was burned; it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that the primary and secondary schools, as well as -- in Bosanski Samac, as well as the village of Zasavica, was being used to isolate and detain large numbers, hundreds, of non-Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that they were being used for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Simo Zaric gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on April 2nd, 1998, which is Exhibit 141? And when he was questioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that this is a repeated question. I mean, we have already established that the witness doesn't know when Mr. Zaric gave his interview to the Office of the Prosecutor. Maybe my colleague would ask it in a better way, but asking again this -- are you aware that Mr. Zaric gave his interview on the 2nd of April. He didn't know that, particularly about the date. If you want to quote it, I have no problem with that. But asking him this way ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. I think you understand what Mr. Lazarevic is saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, that Simo Zaric has given a statement and in the statement he was asked, at page 43, "How was it then that you know the Crisis Staff is the one who made the decision to isolate these people in Zasavica?" Answer: "It was no secret. It was a well-known fact. Everything that was decide was well known. For instance, that people were going to be taken to Crkvina and that they were detained in two schools, it was all well known. There was no secret about it." Sir, are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would give that statement indicating the Crisis Staff was involved in the isolation of non-Serb civilians if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why Mr. Zaric gave such a statement, but I can say that this was not a generally-known fact. Had it been known, I would certainly know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zaric further states at page 40, "The Samac Crisis Staff had decided at some point -- I know that. I don't know when the decision was made -- on the isolation of Croats, and they were then -- a number of them were taken from Samac and put in these -- placed in these abandoned houses in Zasavica or also made to -- for them accommodation to be provided by those persons already living there. I don't think it was a camp in a typical sense because they were able to walk about. But certainly I know about the decision, and this was a very unfortunate one, very bad decision made by the Crisis Staff." Question: "So it was the Crisis Staff in Samac at some point decided that the Croats living in Samac municipality should be removed from their homes and sent to Zasavica?" "This was not exclusively for Croats." This is the answer. "This was not exclusively for Croats, because there were also some Muslim families there, I believe. The decision was made following the imprisonment of those people in the Odzak area. I think it wasn't just for Croats." "Q. But the people were forced to leave their homes and go to Zasavica. Is that right? "A. Yes. "Q. And what happened to the homes and the property they left behind? "A. Yes. This is what happened. And first what happened is the authorities in Samac had put in these houses and flats some of their new key people that they had from elsewhere. Later on Serbs from Krajina and refugees from elsewhere were placed in these houses. As far as their property is concerned, it has the same fate as the property as many others as I've mentioned before, is that the paramilitaries and all those criminals thoroughly looted many houses and flats in Samac and many, many goods were taken away." Sir, are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would make that statement concerning your Crisis Staff's involvement in the isolation of non-Serbs if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the reasons due to which Mr. Simo Zaric gave such a statement, but what I do know is that the Crisis Staff did not have such authority, nor did it ever deal with that issue, and it did not ever adopt any decision on the isolation of non-Serb -- of the non-Serb population, because that simply was not in the job description of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Miroslav Tadic also gave a statement indicating massive arrests occurred? At his interview on March -- on the 26th of March, 1998, which is Exhibit P138: "Q. But Mr. Tadic, you know that dozens, if not hundreds of men were arrested in that week after the takeover and were detained at the police station and at camps in Samac. Some of these were old men, as you like to describe yourself, much older than you. At least one of these men was a Catholic priest. Why were all these people being arrested? You mean to tell me that every single one of these men was arrested because they were concealing weapons? "A. No. I was talking about the first days of the war. I was talking about those days. I was talking about the 18th, the 19th, the 20th, those first days after the war. I think that not more than 30 were arrested then and there's no question that a large number of people were arrested then. What you're talking about, the mass arrest that took place, I think, possibly a month later. "Q. Do you know of any reason why Miroslav Tadic would indicate that there was a mass arrest that took place in May if it wasn't true, sir? "A. I'm not aware of the reasons why Mr. Miroslav Tadic would give such a statement." Sir, I'd like you to look at Exhibit P82, please. Are you familiar with that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this document later, maybe a couple of months ago in the files or the archives of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know who Mitar Mitrovic is?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mitar Mitrovic was the head of the professional staff of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was also the secretary to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the secretary of the Municipal Assembly of Samac and the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he responded to a letter from his holiness Patriarch Pavle, correct, in this letter?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was unusual. However, he allowed himself to reply to the Synod and to his holiness Patriarch Pavle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And the Patriarch was the highest member of the Orthodox church. Wasn't that what his position was back then, the highest member -- or held the highest position?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. His holiness Patriarch Pavle is the highest person in the Serbian Orthodox Church.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And in that letter he said to Patriarch Pavle --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am objecting to the formulation of the question, page 49, line 14. The Prosecutor said that that was a reply to the letter of His Holiness Patriarch Pavle. Whereas, in this letter itself I can see that this is simply an appeal addressed to him. That's why I wouldn't like to Prosecutor to put a question that is not based on the content of the document itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour, if you allow me, we should go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sure. That's fine. I wasn't going to go into any names but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But on the ELMO, we have some names.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. You can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: For the record, this is from the November 16th, 1999 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "Can we come to the subject of isolation" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Before we -- before my colleague proceed, what interview are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This is the Omri, O-m-r-i, the international press interview which was provided to you last week which we discussed, which you mentioned last week that you had received it -- I'm sorry, the week before. "Can we come to the subject of isolation. Where were the locations of these camps? Who controlled them? Who selected the people to be isolated? Were there any lists? And if so, who prepared them? Answer by Mr. Zaric -- or the defendant Zaric, "All arrests were conducted by the civilian police. But Miljkovic collaborated with this police. Chief of police Todorovic decided who was to be isolated. I don't think there were any lists. The civilian police based its selection simply on national ethnic grounds. On May 8th the Odzak camp --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner. Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I really have no problem about the content of what is my colleague quoting. It is just a matter of principle. This document was disclosed after the end of the Prosecution case, so I do believe that it is unfair to be -- that this document can be used here impeaching this witness statement. Particularly, having in mind that this document was in possession of the Prosecution for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic. The fact that the document was discovered after the Prosecution case does not really matter. You can deal with it in re-examination or during your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, it further states, "On May 8th, the Odzak camp was established and the War Presidency," which should be referring to the Crisis Staff, "here decided for the mass isolation of Croats but also Muslims to create the possibility for exchange. They also detained plenty of my unit, but as time passed my influence diminished and theirs increased and I could do much less." Sir, are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would indicate that it was the Crisis Staff or the War Presidency -- at that time the Crisis Staff -- that decided for the mass arrests of Croats and Muslims to create the possibility of exchange? Why he would say that if it wasn't true, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be fair for this witness to have this document in front of him on the language that he understands or at least that we could -- we could have this kind of translation in order to -- to discuss that matter with this witness. I mean, how we can -- how we can even know what the line of -- I mean, it's a matter of fairness finally. Otherwise, it's an ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But Mr. Weiner had said that this document was given to the Defence, so it can't be an ambush. If you are talking about the document being given to the witness for him to read, that's a different matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we cannot translate that for the sake of witness testimony or -- it's not in B/C/S language. It's an absolutely useless document for these purposes. So maybe -- maybe at least we could have a copy of that document on the ELMO so that we can follow the relevant part and then to follow the translation, et cetera, because otherwise it's just something which is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't receive any summaries or statements of what these Defence witnesses will say. I have to guess ahead of time what these people are going to say and try and come up with a cross-examination. Today he started to testify about isolation. How should we know what to -- what to translate, what to be prepared for if we're not getting proper discovery? I can't be prepared to -- to supply translation of this if I don't even know it's going to be rise raised today. We're not getting proper discovery, and this is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But there is an easy --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me. It is not -- this witness was -- I mean, we have a summary of this witness as a member of Crisis Staff, Your Honour. And he will speak about every events about the activities of the Crisis Staff. It is not fair what the counsel just said. It is not fair. Because he's a member of the Crisis Staff, so tell us -- he can tell -- or the P exhibits, the decisions of the Crisis Staff, including -- and this issue of isolation. It's not fair, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, Mr. Weiner. What is required here is to have a translation into B/C/S of the matters you say one of the defendants said to whoever was interviewing him so that the witness can understand what was said in B/C/S and then you can put your questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: But once again, Your Honour, if we don't know ahead of time what these people are going to testify about, we can't be prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, I think we've discussed enough about the summaries. And in fairness to the witness, you cannot treat him like that because of maybe a mistake by the Defence counsel. But I believe that what Mr. Pantelic has said about the summaries are being sufficient. I think the Trial Chamber would agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because there are so many points that the summaries indicate that the witness is going to cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, I was just going to finish off with a statement from Stevan Todorovic -- or actually, the decision, the judgment of Stevan Todorovic, where he admits to the isolation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So the questions about -- in reference to the Omri interview, we don't deal -- you will withdraw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I would just leave him with that and ask him does he know any reason why Simo Zaric would say that, that the Crisis Staff was involved in the isolation if it wasn't true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But that is a point that the Defence was making, that the witness hasn't seen that document and if at all -- it's in English. Can we have it translated into B/C/S or at least translated. So what -- when you read a statement from that document, let the interpreters translate so that the witness can understand what is in the document. And then you can ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll just finish with the Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So that evidence on the Omri interview is withdrawn?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And just finish with the Stevan Todorovic, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Finally, sir, are you aware that Stevan Todorovic has admitted to implementing a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac requiring all people of Croatian nationality in the area to be isolated and taken to vital facilities in the town and in the villages? Are you aware of that, that Stevan Todorovic has admitted to being involved with the Crisis Staff's decision to isolate Croat citizens?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of what Mr. Stevan Todorovic has admitted to, but I do know that the Crisis Staff never passed a decision of that nature. Therefore, no isolation whatsoever, no placing of people in certain facilities and so on. The Crisis Staff never passed such a decision, and Mr. Todorovic was not able to implement that decision. Maybe he implemented some kind of his own decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has already replied. But I would like to ask that the Prosecutor be instructed to say when did Stevan Todorovic admit to this. I don't know whether he admitted to this in the proceedings or in the courtroom, but if he admitted to this in the course of an interview, then I don't think that can be introduced as evidence. So could the Prosecutor please tell us when was this admitted by Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That was during his plea of guilt. As part of his plea of guilt, he admitted to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So my question to you is: Based on Stevan Todorovic, your police chief, admission to being involved in the Crisis Staff's decision to isolate the Croat population and based on the statements of Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic, do you still wish to maintain that you were not aware of the isolation policy issued by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I wish to maintain my position. I wish to maintain the truth, and the truth is as follows --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question -- the question to you was, and I will read it again: Based on Stevan Todorovic, your police chief's admission to being involved in the Crisis Staff's decision to isolate the Croat population and based on the statements of Simo Zaric and Miroslav Tadic, do you still wish to maintain that you were not aware of the isolation policy issued by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff did not enforce that kind of policy, so it's not a matter of me being aware or not. I just that the Crisis Staff never enforced such policy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in addition to the arrests, were you aware that large numbers of non-Serb civilians were being held at the police station, at the Territorial Defence building, at the primary and secondary schools in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about large number of arrests, either in my official capacity or in any other capacity. All I can say is that I assume there had been some arrests. But as to their numbers, I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're just assuming that there had been arrests, period. You're not aware of any arrests?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of arrests. But all I know about the arrests stems from the television programme which was broadcast by Radio Television Serbia, Novi Sad studio, 10 days after the breakout of hostility in Samac municipality. All I know about arrests was learned from that programme at the time. Later on, of course, I learned about them from the press, from television, and from the book of Dragan Lukac, as I've mentioned to you already. But at the time all I knew about it I learned from that television programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So when you say "later on," you're trying to tell us you weren't aware of the arrests in Bosanski Samac till years later.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. That television programme had a report saying that there were arrests. So I knew about the arrests. But as to their numbers ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Other than that television programme at the end of April, you were not aware of any arrests in Bosanski Samac -- any other arrests to the end -- till a few years later when you read Dragan Lukac's book and read something in the press or saw something on television, years later? Is that what you're trying to say?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm trying to say that I knew that there were arrests. But as to their scope, the numbers, who was arrested, why, I thought that all of these matters were in the competencies of the police and the investigative authorities. Therefore, I did not dwell on it. As to the numbers and the essence of it, I learned about it later through books and the press.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: When you say "later," when are you talking about? What year?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 1996, 1997, after the war was finished and once the situation was improved and one could talk about such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you're saying you were never aware that hundreds of people were being held at various facilities in Bosanski Samac back in 1992? You were not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that hundreds of people were imprisoned, because that's a large number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that Dragan Lukac, the police chief, was arrested and being held?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that from his book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you were not aware in 1992 that Dragan Lukac, your police chief, was being held?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw on television Izet Izetbegovic and Omer Nalic, and I can't remember any other names. I don't remember whether Dragan Lukac was there as well then. However, I remember the first two persons I mentioned. I remember seeing them on the television programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And do you remember Sulejman Tihic was being held?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. However, I do not exclude the possibility that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So you, at this point, don't recall knowing in 1992 that the president of the SDA was being held -- had been arrested and was being held in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that because the police method, their operative work, the reasons for arrest is something that I didn't know about it, nor do I know about it nowadays.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that non-Serb civilian prisoners were being beaten?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the police methods. I didn't know how they operated. I learned of this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, at the time were you aware in 1992 that non-Serb civilian prisoners were being beaten in Bosanski Samac? Were you aware of that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that they had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that non-Serb civilians were being tortured in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the entire treatment of them, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that other than even the Crkvina incident, non-Serb civilians were being murdered? Were you aware of that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That Serb civilians were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Non-Serb civilians. Non-Serb civilians who were being held as prisoners were murdered in 1992. Other than the Crkvina incident, were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that any civilians were killed, either Serb, Croat, or Muslim civilians. I wasn't aware of any killing of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our lunch break and continue at 14.30 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, in 1992, were you aware that prisoners were being held at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that I saw this TV programme of TV Serbia, TV Novi Sad, and it is in this programme that I saw that there were prisoners, so I knew there were prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No. I'm saying being held at the police station. Were you aware that they were being held at the SUP, the police station?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never at the police station, and I cannot confirm anything as an eyewitness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that prisoners were being held at the Territorial Defence building?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of prisoners being held at the Territorial Defence building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that prisoners were being held at the primary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that prisoners were being held at the primary school building, and I could not believe that because the primary school building had been set on fire and therefore was unusable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In the gymnasium of the primary school, were you aware that prisoners were being held, in the gymnasium of that primary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware that they were being held in the gymnasium of the primary school, or did I know what the condition of that gymnasium was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, were you aware that prisoners were being held at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware that prisoners were being held at the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware that prisoners were being held in the village of Zasavica?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never could I notice any such thing, and I did pass along the Samac-Modrica road. I never noticed any such thing in Zasavica. Viewed from that road, that village looked quite usual to me, just like all the other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were the information officer for the Crisis Staff. You weren't aware of any of this information?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no press releases coming in from the appropriate authorities to the information service, so it is not that I could have made them public through the information service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as part of your position on the Crisis Staff, did you ever visit the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal building? I went there seldom, very seldom. What I remember is one particular time I went there. I think it was in May 1992. I can describe that particular time when I went there, if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: How many times did you visit the municipal building in the month of May?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember this one time when I went there, which left a profound impact on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Did you visit the municipal building in the month of April?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the month of April I was not in the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: As the press officer for the Crisis Staff, the person who distributed the news to the press agencies and the public, you never went to the municipal building to see what was going on in April or May other than one time?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not necessary for me to go there because there were people, journalists, who went there or perhaps they also received information by telephone with regard to a particular area, and then perhaps that is how they made this information public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So people used the telephones or the press used the telephones in April and May to transact business or exchange information.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inter alia, of course when the telephone lines were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, did you hear from anyone -- you must have moved around the city. Did you hear from any doctors, nurses, police officers, soldiers, municipal officials, municipal worker, residents, anyone about the mistreatment of prisoners in the small town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one said anything to me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at document -- Exhibit P127. We've referred to it as the 13 signatories document. It's signed by the defendant Simo Zaric and 12 other officers. I'd invite your attention to page 2, paragraph 5. Do you see where it says "fifth paragraph" on there? Would you count down to the third sentence in that paragraph, the fifth paragraph. It starts, "The massive ...." Do you see it? It says, "The massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims followed without any criteria and some of the prisoners were subjected to measures such as abuse, torture, and even killing, characteristic only of war criminals of Ustasha origin." Based on this document -- yes. Is that what it says, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did that third sentence start?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'll read it again.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My third sentence reads as follows: "They were joined very soon by," et cetera, et cetera. That's the third sentence that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The next sentence. I'll read it again: "The massive arrests and isolation of Croats and Muslims followed without any criteria and some of the prisoners were subjected to measures such as abuse, torture, and even killing, characteristic only of war criminals of Ustasha origin." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document, it says that this is information which is within the command of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade, and I did not have the opportunity of seeing this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: Is that correct, what I just read to you? Did I read it correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read it correctly, but I don't know whether that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: My question to you is: Do you know of any reason why these 13 military officers would have made that statement about the abuse or mistreatment of prisoners if it wasn't true? Do you know of any reason, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to read this document in its entirety and then I could give an answer as to what the intention was. I know that all the way up to the end of the war there was this conflict between the civilian and the military authorities. And as I've already said, this culminated in 1993, September 1993. And Mr. Karadzic and Mladic had some kind of an ongoing conflict throughout the war. It is in that context that I understand this particular information. But I must admit that I haven't read the whole document, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you find it odd that you as the information officer of the Crisis Staff was not aware of the mistreatment of prisoners? However, even the military, Simo Zaric and 12 other military officers, were not only aware of it. They filed a document concerning it. Don't you find that odd?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what seems even stranger to me is the following: If this was known about, why did the investigation authorities and the other competent authorities of the military, why didn't they take any action? Probably they had some reason. I was not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Isn't it because that the military and the civilian authorities wanted this to happen? Isn't that why nothing was done, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not say that that could be the answer. I do not believe that this is what the military or civilian authorities wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, apparently from that letter from the 13th officers some of the military officers did not want the mistreatment going -- continuing in your municipality. But let's continue, sir. Were you -- are you aware that Stevan Todorovic at his guilty plea has admitted to repeated beatings, sexual assaults, and murder at the police station, at the Territorial Defence building, at the primary and secondary school in Bosanski Samac? Are you aware of that, sir? And that's from the sentencing judgment, at pages 11 through 12, 31 July 2002. Are you aware that he's made those admissions, sir, to that type of conduct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is quite possible that Mr. Stevan Todorovic admitted to what he had done himself. However, what he did was obviously not transparent enough. It did not reach other people who perhaps should have known about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, just my question is: Are you aware that Stevan Todorovic has admitted to that conduct, as I mentioned? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that he admitted to something. But what it was specifically is something that I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, but you're the information officer. You were the information officer on the Crisis Staff. Wasn't it your job to know what these people were doing and what these people are admitted to, what crimes they're admitted to? That affects your community.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for information pertaining to military matters and police matters, this information came from the military and police authorities. So what they submitted was then made public. As for some kind of investigative journalism, that could not be carried out in a war situation. I assume that you are referring to investigative journalism, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, sir. What I'm saying is you are the person who provides information to the press. You're the person that they turn to. You're the liaison to the press. It's your job to know these things, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only me. There was also the editor-in-chief of the radio station. Then also there was the editor-in-chief of the "Koridor" newspaper. I was not the person who condensed this power in the field of information, because the law on information precisely regulates the authorities and powers of individual persons in the media. However, it is certain that I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to get to the "Koridor" newspaper and the radio very shortly. But I also want to ask you: Are you aware that your cousin, Milan Simic, has admitted to torturing five non-Serb civilians at the primary school in Bosanski Samac and that these incidents occurred while he was president of the executive council and you were a member of the Crisis Staff or War Presidency? Are you aware of that, that your cousin has pled guilty to these, has admitted to these crimes?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of what he had admitted to. But what I am well aware of is that my cousin, Milan Simic, never spoke in front of me about these actions that you have just referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, based on the admissions of your cousin, your cousin, that he tortured five people; based on the admissions of Stevan Todorovic, that he beat, tortured, and murdered people; based on the documents from the military; based on the statements of Simo Zaric, will you agree with me that the prisoners in Bosanski Samac were abused and mistreated in 1992 while they were detained, the non-Serb civilians, mistreated during detention?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree on the following: That neither Mr. Todorovic nor Mr. Milan Simic nor anyone else who had committed such things, never spoke about this in my presence. That is what I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. My question is: Based on the statements of your cousin, Milan Simic, who has admitted to torturing five non-Serb civilians at the primary school; Stevan Todorovic, who has admitted to beatings, sexual assaults, and murder at the SUP, at the TO, at the primary school, at the secondary school; based on the information from the military; based on the statements of Simo Zaric; based on all of these things that I've presented to you, all of these admissions, will you now agree that non-Serb civilians were beaten and abused and mistreated while they were detained in Bosanski Samac in 1992? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that that's the way it was, but I really did not see any of this or did any one of them tell me about these actions. But I can assume that if that is what they admitted to, then that is probably the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned the radio station. Isn't it true that that radio station was broadcasting information concerning the arrest of non-Serb civilians in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That radio station did not broadcast information about the arrest of non-Serb civilians in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that that radio station was broadcasting information concerning the takeover, the activities of the 4th Detachment, the arrests and the reasons for the arrests of non-civilians in Bosanski Samac? Isn't it true that the radio station was broadcasting all of that information?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's an analysis -- I mean, the radio station functioned in a way that was quite different. I mean, some kind of a press release and a lot of music. The first day it was broadcasting for about an hour, a bit over an hour. And then some of the equipment -- the transmission equipment did not work and then it took about 20 days for it to start functioning normally. And that is why this information leaflet had been started, so that this shortage of information could be made up for.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. Excuse me. Sir, isn't it true that not only did the radio station list the persons who were being arrested. That newspaper indicated who was being arrested and being detained in Bosanski Samac and the reasons for it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That would have been too primitive a type of work in the field of information. People who worked in that area would not go below their professional standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, as information officer for the Crisis Staff, were you not aware that the radio station and the newspaper, that local news bulletin, was listing the persons who were arrested, notifying the public of the persons who were arrested and the reasons for their detention? Isn't that true? And you should know that as chief of information.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that is not the way it was. So the information leaflet and the radio station did not publish any names of arrested persons or were they involved in any similar matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know the man sitting over there in the middle, Miroslav Tadic? Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He's --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked together at a school for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: He was a fellow member of the Crisis Staff with you, a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Tadic held a position at the Crisis Staff at the time when he was appointed head of civilian protection staff, and he held that position until the War Presidency was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, Miroslav Tadic was asked when he gave a statement on the 26th of March, 1998, Exhibit 138, page 43 - for the Court's edification - and he was asked, "How did you know -- how did you learn about these detainees and the reason for their arrest?" And he stated the following: "Well, just talking in town. I read it in the newspapers. There was a newspaper which was publishing articles. And of course Radio Samac. Radio Samac also had these -- was also broadcasting news. The weapons were found at such and such a person's house or such and such a person -- so that's how we knew." Do you know of any reason why Miroslav Tadic would indicate that he got his news from Radio Samac and the newspaper if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is obvious that Mr. Miroslav Tadic got things confused in his recollection, and this statement of his is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the reasons, that's something that I stated in my introductory part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's continue. Your cousin, Milan Simic, president of the executive council, he was also interviewed on March 2nd, 1998. And at page 12 he was asked how he knew why people were being held at the TO. And how does he know? There was a proclamation broadcast on Radio Samac all the time for all those possessing illegal weapons to surrender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another objection, Your Honour, that is based on a principle. I would like to know what the position of the Trial Chamber is where the Prosecutor can in fact put forward part of the statement that was not admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, when you ask a statement, it is the same as you ask any other question. The witness can deny it. He can say, "I feel that there's a reason for prejudice. I disagree with it. I don't know why he would say it. He's wrong." He can agree with it. He can say it's an absolute lie. It's like any other statement, whether you read a statement or whether you confront a person with it. I've asked him is he aware of any reason -- I'm going to ask him is he aware of any reason that Milan Simic would say it if it wasn't true. I'm going to ask him about the bias and prejudice that Simic would have to make such a statement of that kind. He's claiming this person was in charge of the informational system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. But the point raised by Mr. Lukic, that it wasn't admitted into evidence, the statement -- the interview that you've been reading. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Correct. But many statements aren't that we've had -- that we've questioned witnessed aren't introduced into evidence. It's strictly a -- you ask the person strictly as a question. If they agree it to, then their agreement is in evidence. If they deny it, it's not, it's not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back to what prompted me to put my last question. I realise that the decision of a different Trial Chamber not to put to witness statements of other witnesses or other persons is so that not to confuse that witness. And this is what I understood your position to be during the Prosecution case. But now I'm confused. It seems to me that now we are quietly introducing to the witness a statement of another person, be it in the form of an interview, of some other kind of statement. But in this way, there is an attempt to impeach this witness and to question his credibility. I think that in such cases a question needs to be formulated in very specific terms, rather than put another statement to the witness. I think that was the basis of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner. The statement which -- the interview which you referred to by Mr. Milan Simic was not admitted into evidence, unlike the other interviews for the other defendants in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. I'll stick to admitted matters or matters in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because it is only fair. Then the -- the point that the Defence would have known how to deal with that regarding the interviews they've had with their witnesses, if that document or the interview was on record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll stick with that, in public documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that Simo Zaric -- the defendant Simo Zaric has provided a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor -- actually, I'll let you know -- or for the Court. It's the statement of April 2nd, 1998, at 141. And at that -- and on page 12 he discusses on at least four -- where he discusses on at least four occasions the radio station. And let me read that to you. "That morning I wrote, because I was in charge of the morale of the 4th Detachment -- I wrote an article and it was read out and broadcast over the radio three times and since then." And he later goes on to explain that he was chastised for this radio announcement relating to the 4th Detachment that was broadcasted multiple times. Do you know of any reason why Simo Zaric would make a statement that he -- that on morning of the 17th he broadcasted a statement at least three or more times over the radio as to what was happening in Bosanski Samac if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is now that I learned that Mr. Zaric developed the programme together with editor-in-chief. I didn't know that before. If he did that, then that is something they knew nothing of before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And further --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And further, sir, he also indicated that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, just -- I do apologise, my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's -- just a correction, I believe, in the transcript. Page 76, line 9. The last part of the sentence, it should be, "Then that is something that I knew nothing of before," because the word "they" is a little bit ambiguous, and I don't believe that this witness said "they," instead of "I." Maybe you can clarify that with the witness, just for the sake of clarity in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner, you can see that response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Page 76, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: You stated "if he did that, then that is something they knew nothing of before." Who are you referring to they being?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I meant Mr. Zaric and editor-in-chief of the radio station. If they broadcast that information, and I knew nothing of it, then they were basically in charge of the programme for that day. I simply knew nothing of it. Even now I don't know what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Were you aware, sir, that Sulejman Tihic, president of the SDA, was brought to the radio station and told that he should speak to the Muslims and tell them to accept the creation of the Serbian municipality? Were you aware of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that Sulejman Tihic was ever a guest of Radio Samac -- the radio station Samac. Could you clarify this, please. Who brought him there?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, while he was detained, after he was arrested, he was forcibly brought to the radio station. Isn't it true that he was forcibly brought to the radio station and made to go on and give a statement to the public, basically to the Muslim public, asking them to accept the rule of the Serbian Municipality of Samac?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, and I cannot believe that either for a very simple technical reason: Had this been really intended, it would have been much easier to tape his statement and then later on broadcast it. I don't see why he would have to come to the radio station personally, because something like that simply wasn't necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, well, let me discuss this. Simo Zaric has given another statement. On page 15 of Exhibit 141, in his interview with the Office of the Prosecutor, and he tells how he was chastised by Stevan Todorovic and Blagoje Simic. "While with Todorovic and Simic, they told me that I was no longer any factor of power, that they were in power, that I was nothing and that my job was to look after the borders and that I should not be meddling into the affairs in the town. They also said to me 'why did you put that announcement of the 4th Detachment in the radio?' By that time, that was going out on the radio was there press staff about the creation of the Serbian Municipality of Samac. Also what they did later on was to bring -- then I learned they were bringing Sulejman Tihic, the president of the SDA, who had gone on the radio to say that the Muslims should accept the creation of the Serbian municipality, and I believed this supposed speech of Mr. Tihic had been written and directed by Todorovic and Simic." Sir, do you know of any reason that Simo Zaric would indicate that Tihic was using the radio, that he had broadcasted announcements on the radio, and that the Crisis Staff, the Serbian Municipality, was using the radio if it wasn't true? Do you know of any reason that he would make that statement?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I truly don't know who chastised whom, whether it was Simo Zaric, Stevan Todorovic, and Blagoje Simic, or vice versa. Blagoje Simic and Stevan Todorovic chastising Simo Zaric. I really am not familiar with their relationship. What I do know about it is that I have no information to the effect that Sulejman Tihic was a guest of Radio Samac, and I've already told you the reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, my question was: Do you know of any reason why Simo Zaric would indicate that Tihic was using the radio, that he broadcasted announcements on the radio, and that the Crisis Staff, the Serbian Municipality, was using the radio if it wasn't true? That's my question. Do you know of any reason he would make that statement concerning the use of the radio if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any reason that could prompt him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's continue. You testified today and yesterday concerning the military and the lack of involvement of the Crisis Staff in military decisions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff never got involved in the military matters and military functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a man by the name of Colonel Mico Djurdjevic? I think you mentioned him on your first day of testimony, Mico Djurdjevic? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And he was -- he initially replaced Colonel Nikolic as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade. He held the position just less than a week. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what went on within the military. I know Colonel Djurdjevic from the incident involving interparty meeting. As for his other activities within the military, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that the Crisis Staff was -- played the key role in the removal of Colonel Djurdjevic, the Crisis Staff with you serving as a member?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff had a problem after the request was submitted to ensure that telephone connections are established. And as to having such powers, as to actually be able to influence the appointment of a military commander, that is simply not true, because military commanders were appointed by relevant military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall a meeting in May of 1992 at the Crisis Staff offices involving Colonel Djurdjevic? At this meeting was Blagoje Simic, Stevan Todorovic, Bozo Ninkovic, yourself, Crni, and volunteers from Serbia. Isn't it true that there was that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that such a meeting was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, do you recall at a meeting, sir, that the Crisis Staff indicated to Colonel Djurdjevic that they were not pleased with his actions and that you were sitting there when that happened?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That the Crisis Staff indicated that? In which form? Was it in a written form? Was it verbally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: In a discussion they told him that they were not pleased with his actions and that they wanted the colonel to change his attitude towards Crni and the volunteers from Serbia. Do you recall that conversation with Colonel Djurdjevic at the Crisis Staff offices, with armed volunteers from Serbia being present?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not meet Colonel Djurdjevic throughout the entire war. I especially didn't talk to him. Perhaps I did meet him -- did see him passing by. However, I never was involved, nor do I know that somebody from the Crisis Staff was involved in his appointment or removal from office or any other such activities. Simply speaking, the Crisis Staff had no authority to appoint military commanders. That's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that after that meeting with the Crisis Staff members, including yourself, that a private meeting was convened with Colonel Djurdjevic, Stevan Todorovic, and Blagoje Simic, that a short while later Crni entered the meeting, and an hour later they left the meeting, where Todorovic announced that Crni was now the brigade commander and that Colonel Djurdjevic was dismissed? Isn't that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate in private meetings of that nature; therefore, I am not aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to refer to another statement given by the defendant Simo Zaric. For the Court, it was on April 1st, 1998, Exhibit 140, and it concerns this incident at the Crisis Staff. At pages 34 through 35 he talks about Colonel Mico Djurdjevic, and I'll read it to you. I'll read it slowly. Page 35. It says: "He," in referring to Colonel Djurdjevic. "He did not want any improper actions, incident, looting, anything like that. He was very much opposed to it. Now he only stayed in this post for seven days; probably because of the attitude he had. And I can tell you how he was replaced. Now, he was replaced and this was actually initiated by the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac municipality, by the leadership. I would say that two people who had influenced in his replacement was Mr. Simic and Mr. Todorovic. He wanted to have control over the army and the command of the army. A few days before he was replaced, Djurdjevic talked to me on the phone and said he'd come and visit our area of responsibility, positions, and where the army was, and I was then told during the day that he had come and that I should go and say hello to him at the Crisis Staff. When I arrived at the office of the Crisis Staff, I found there Mr. Todorovic, president of the Crisis Staff Blagoje Simic, Simeon Simic. He was there. He was still a member. There was Bozo Ninkovic, who also had some kind of position within the Crisis Staff. With them were several armed special operatives in uniforms, in a kind of camouflage uniform, but these were people who had gone through this special training course. These were people not from the Samac town but from the Samac municipality area. They said they had information that people were unhappy about him taking over command. That's how it was presented. And they said they also wanted him to have more cooperation between the civilian authorities and the command. And they also wanted him to change his attitude regarding Crni, the paramilitary leader, and the group of volunteers from Serbia. I think that then Mr. Djurdjevic estimated the situation was becoming threatening for him. Then he asked for the meeting to resume without nobody else in the room except Todorovic, Simic, and himself. After about an hour, they were joined in their meeting by Dragan Djordjevic, Crni. I later found out that this was his name. So there were four of them. And after about one hour of discussion, Todorovic stepped out of the office and said that everything had been arranged, that there would be a new commander of the brigade, that there would be Dragan Djordjevic, Crni, that it had all been arranged. I have to say I was completely shocked and I was not the only one and there were some other people except for those people who were part of the script making, so they were not surprised." Sir, this statement here by Simo Zaric describes a meeting of the Crisis Staff which resulted in the dismissal of Colonel Djurdjevic and it indicates you were there for part of that meeting. Do you know of any reason why Simo Zaric would make this statement if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say the following: In the statement that you've just read out, there is a lot of imagination, and I know this imagination very well. It has to do with the times past, in the times when they were set up court proceedings. And everything contained in that statement is a product of somebody's imagination. Let's ask ourselves following how come that Colonel Djurdjevic, who had at his disposal military police, soldiers, the entire brigade, got so scared of unarmed people from the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: Are you aware of any reason why Simo Zaric would make that statement if it wasn't true? Is your statement -- it's a lie? Is that your statement? Or is it -- or do you know of no reason that he would make it?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Out of civility, I wouldn't use the term "lie." But there is no doubt that there's quite a lot of imagination there. And also there is no doubt that that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like you to look at Exhibit P127 again. Sir, on the first page, the third paragraph, please. It says "third,".

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, I already had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. We're going to look at it again. The first page, again, do you see where the paragraph begins with the word "third"? Do you see that paragraph, sir? It's on the bottom of the first, maybe on the top of the second page.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The third.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes. All right. Let me read it.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Do you see that this document also refers to the Crisis Staff's involvement in the removal of Colonel Djurdjevic? Let's see what it says. "Third, the temporary takeover of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade by Colonel Djurdjevic can be regarded as a brave act worthy of respect given to that. Lieutenant Nikolic in his offices had left these people completely unprotected. However, Colonel Djurdjevic managed to keep this post for only a few days because after he tried to introduce more military order and discipline in the brigade, put an end to certain activities which had directly helped sour relations within the brigade, and dismiss Crni from his post of commander of the special battalion and appoint a new commander, and after he garnered unqualified support for this from the members of the command, battalion officers, and some members of the government and Crisis Staff, a sudden reversal took place with an incident staged in the office of the president of the War Presidency, where an interview was first held with Colonel Djurdjevic in the presence of an armed group of commandos, to be followed by an interview attended by Dr. Blagoje Simic, president of the War Presidency; Stevan Todorovic, chief of the SJB, Public Security Station; Crni; and Colonel Djurdjevic, and resulting in their joint agreement that Colonel Djurdjevic be dismissed. Dragan Djordjevic, aka Crni, was soon appointed commander of the brigade and was promoted overnight from private to lieutenant colonel for this post." Sir, did I read that correctly? Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you've read that very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know of any reason why these 13 officers would indicate that the Crisis Staff was involved in the removal of Colonel Djurdjevic if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why. If the majority of the command of the brigade gave their support or backing, why he didn't stay. Who could have removed him if he enjoyed such support within the military structures. That's one thing. Also, I don't know who could have been promoted overnight to lieutenant colonel rank. The Crisis Staff was not able to promote anyone, nor did it have any authority to do that. So everything happened --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, apparently the Crisis Staff did it according to that statement. So my question to you again is: Do you know of any reason why those 13 officers would indicate that the Crisis Staff was involved in the removal of Colonel Djurdjevic and subsequently the promotion of Crni, the paramilitary, if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are perhaps some settling of accounts within the military circles. This is how I interpret it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And that's your speculation.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have another answer, because the information by the secret services or the security services were not available to me. That was not the kind of information that I could receive. But obviously something was cooking there, but I cannot claim with certainty anything about that, but I also would like to know the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Maybe the answer is, sir -- or maybe the answer is because it's true, the Crisis Staff was involved in that action. But sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, was the Crisis Staff involved in further -- was the Crisis Staff involved in further decisions relating to military affairs?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say it again. The Crisis Staff is a civilian organ of authority and did not have any power to get involved; particularly not during the war to get involved into the military structure or the decision-making process within the army. It did not have the authority to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, will you turn to page 3 of that same document and look at paragraph 7, please. Okay. Do you see where it says "seventh," paragraph 7, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see what it says there. "The War Presidency or executive committee of Samac municipality made certain efforts to help the army as much as it was able, with materiel supplies and funds for the purchase of certain equipment for the soldiers. This is certainly the positive side of the picture. And influential individuals in the civilian authorities believed and acted accordingly that in return for all of the material and financial assistance they had the right to interfere most directly with the military authorities, formulate personal policy at the level of the brigade, and install at its helm only obedient commanders who would carry out some of their private policies through military channels. Consequently, our brigade has changed six commanders since the outbreak of the war to the present day. Some of them holding that post for a few days, and others for several months, depending on whether they were their players or somebody else's. The civilian authorities generally dominated the military authorities except during Crni's period because the civilian authorities turned some brigade commanders into obedient military commanders in a very perfidious manner." Did I read that correctly, sir?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You've read that correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, again, are you aware of any reason -- are you aware of any reason why these 13 military officers would describe the involvement of the War Presidency, the executive committee, in military decision-making if it wasn't true, why they would complain about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you please allow me one comparison which perhaps is not the best but will reflect in the best way or express in the best way what you have asked. It would be the same as if the wolf were complaining that Little Red Riding Hood was abusing him. That was the relationship between the military and the civilian authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, according to this statement, the military authorities are complaining that the Crisis Staff or at that point the War Presidency and the civilian authorities were ruling the military. They were making the major appointments and they were complaining about it. Now, again, I ask you: Are you aware of any reason why these 13 officers would make this statement if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the previous passage it was stated that all members in the command of the brigade agreed. So the army was united. So how is it possible that such a powerful force --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not my question. On redirect you can discuss all you would like, your personal views of the army. My question again: Are you aware of any reason why 13 officers, basically the defendant Simo Zaric and 12 other officers, would indicate that the Crisis Staff was making key decisions for the military if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's something within the army. Their reasons --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have the Prosecutor's question a little bit more specifically, because on page 87, line 11 he's constantly talking about the War Presidency and now he's interpreting his question and using the term "the Crisis Staff." So I think that it would be necessary for the Prosecutor to be more specific here. Because in that part where he quoted the decision, only the War Presidency is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, you understand Mr. Lukic's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, once again, are you aware of any reason why these -- why the defendant Simo Zaric and 12 other military officers would state that the War Presidency or the civilian authorities of Bosanski Samac would be making key decisions affecting the military if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I interpret that by various interests within the army, as such. And if I may, I would also like to illustrate it as follows: I also as a deputy of the municipal assembly was in military detention, and that speaks quite clearly about the influence of the civilian authority over the military structures. But this did not happen in this period that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We won't get into your detention, sir. Let us continue. You've testified yesterday that you were not aware of the reason -- actually, you testified today that you weren't aware of the reason of the arrest and trial of the Serb volunteers or paramilitaries, Crni and Lugar. You just heard gossip, but you weren't aware of the reason. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said something a little different, that they were arrested because of what happened at Crkvina, the horrific crime there. Then I also assumed that in view of the fear of the population, of the citizens regardless of their ethnicity, I assume that there they made some kind of mistake that I didn't know about and that is why they were in investigative detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: So, sir --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All you can make is assumptions. You as the information officer did not receive the information as to why --

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- these people were arrested. Sir, isn't it true that the War Presidency was involved in an incident leading to their arrest, meaning the closing of the Posavina Corridor? Isn't it true that the involvement of the War Presidency led to their arrest or that the War Presidency was involved in an incident with them which led to their arrest?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency did not take part in the arrests or in any incident. Certain units within the army participated for their own reasons that are not known to me, not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: All right. That was not my question. My question probably wasn't -- was a bit vague. Let's take a step back. Are you aware in 1992 Stevan Todorovic and your cousin, Milan Simic, were arrested by the military and held? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. But I don't know for certain whether it was the military authorities or some other structures, paramilitary formations, the police, but I know that they were arrested. That is a fact that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And, sir, are you aware that as a result of the arrest of Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic, the volunteers or paramilitaries from Serbia, as being led by Crni, closed the Posavina Corridor until Stevan Todorovic and Milan Simic were released? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't know whether this was committed by the paramilitary units. Some units did do that. Also, I would not dare here to give any interpretation, since I am not an expert in that field, of what paramilitary units are. That is not something that I am familiar with. But one of the units did participate in that incident. And as far as I remember, it was the special battalion, which was composed of mainly -- perhaps there were some volunteers there, but mainly from the local soldiers. Actually, they were soldiers who were mobilised from the local base, the local resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that this action by Crni and the special battalion was implemented with the blessing of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true at all, because it is simply impossible for the War Presidency to issue a command to any of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could he please be shown document P116. You can leave that other there. We might go back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Sir, what you have in front of you is a four-page document. We refer to it as P116. It's a signed statement of the defendant Blagoje Simic, and it was given to Captain Nikola Tomasevic, an investigative judge, and Prosecutor Captain Bozidar Srdic. I'd invite your attention to the third page, the fifth paragraph. Do you see where it says, "The corridor was closed"? Do you see that, sir? Let me read that.

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: "The corridor was closed after the kidnapping of Milan Simic, the president of the Samac executive board, and Stevan Todorovic, the chief of the Samac municipality Public Security Station. I really do not know why they were arrested. I just know that they were beaten up and the War Presidency has not received to this day any information on why these two men were arrested by the military police. Crni and his assault battalion shut down the corridor with the support of the Samac War Presidency, given subsequent to the closing of the corridor. The Samac War Presidency did not pass any decisions concerning the closing of the corridor, but it supported that action until the release of Simic and Todorovic. The corridor was opened after 18 hours, when Colonel Simic promised that Simic and Todorovic would be released. Civilian policemen did not participate in the closing of the corridor; however, they secured the checkpoints." Sir, did I read that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, this document, which is signed by the defendant Blagoje Simic, indicates that the War Presidency gave the support to Crni and the special battalion for closing that corridor. Do you know of any reason why Blagoje Simic would give this statement right here, this particular statement, if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: SIMEON SIMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the reasons why he gave this statement, but I know that the War Presidency did not support any kind of assault unit. And after that I don't know. It looks as if this is some kind of rebellion within the army, and I don't know what is behind it. If one unit refuses to obey its higher command, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: That's not the question. That's not the issue for the question. My question is: Are you aware of any reason why Blagoje Simic would indicate that the War Presidency supported the closing of the Posavina Corridor if it wasn't true?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. If we are going into this matter, my learned friend should say that my client, Mr. Blagoje Simic, completely denied the truthfulness of this statement. So if we are speaking about this statement before the military investigating judge, then my friend should say also that, on the other hand, Mr. Blagoje Simic would like to deny everything which was said under the specific circumstances, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Blagoje Simic testified about this statement on two days. On day number one he never questioned that paragraph or any other paragraph except two different comments in this statement. It is signed by him. In his statement at the end, he agrees to the truthfulness of this statement. He agrees to this record without any comment and he signed it.
